slides.text: When I bought a new SIM card after moving to Chicago, I started receiving voicemails every Sunday at 11:00 PM from a stranger named Noah. At first, I thought it was a wrong number. Then I realized he was calling his late sister’s old phone just to tell someone about his week—the stray dog he adopted, the promotion he was nervous about, how quiet his apartment felt when it snowed.

I worked the graveyard shift as a late-night jazz radio host, and Noah’s gentle, bruised voice became the anchor of my Sundays. I couldn't bear to change my greeting and break his heart, and I was too afraid to interrupt his ritual. Instead, on my midnight broadcast, I started dedicating songs to the stories he left on my machine—playing Chet Baker the night he said he couldn't sleep.

Four months later, my phone rang at 11:00 PM while I was sitting in the studio booth. Before it could roll to voicemail, I heard my own radio show playing softly in the background of his call. I picked up the receiver, my heart hammering. Across the static, Noah let out a shaky, breathless laugh. 'I knew it was you,' he whispered. 'Tell me what song comes next, and let me buy you coffee when your shift ends.'
